title: I froze one AI-generated goat sprite on day 5 and never regenerated it. 31 days later it's a herd of 25 in a Steam demo
author: Joe_Finback
selftext:
Keeping generated art consistent is the question I see here most, so here's the rule that solved it for my game, and how the rest of a 31-day build went.

**One master, never regenerated.** Every goat in Ledge Goats comes from one 28x21 px sprite. I generated candidates with Codex's image generation, picked one, cleaned it onto a fixed palette, and froze it on day 5. Nothing is allowed to generate a goat after that. I made that call before any art existed.

* **Coats are data, not art.** The master uses a 4-colour ramp, and a shader swaps those 4 colours. 20 coats are one table of 80 hex values.
* **Horns are overlays.** 14 small horn sprites sit on a head anchor. The named goats' horns have to differ from every other horn by at least 2 px or by stroke width, because a pure colour swap can vanish in grayscale.
* **Motion is code, not frames.** A state machine (rest, crouch, leap, land) moves the one sprite, and each goat has its own rest countdown, so the herd never hops in sync. Beyond horns and bells, the only extra goat art is two lean poses and a warm-coat overlay.
* **Icons reuse master pixels** at whole-number scales, so the goat on an achievement is the same goat. The only exceptions are the painted Steam capsule and a 16 px icon I reduced by hand.

The first image is the master on top and all 20 coats below, rendered straight from the game files.

**Mountains are generated, but pinned.** 7 real peaks in 35 segments of 192x320. Each candidate's seed is fixed by its slot, so a rerun reproduces it. Then a converter snaps every pixel onto that peak's palette and a script finishes it. No hand repainting.

**Code: specs first, agents second.** Every system starts as a written spec. A coding agent (mostly Claude Code) builds it on a branch, a second pass reviews it adversarially, and it only merges through a test gate (281 test files so far). It wasn't smooth. Some specs got stuck after three repair attempts and needed a ruling, which I delegated to a separate "conductor" agent. And re-running the gate at merge time caught a null crash the branch tests had missed.

[The free demo is the first peak, Kosciuszko](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5572200/Ledge_Goats/)

What's your rule for keeping generated art consistent across a whole game?

comments.author: stolenyourgf
comments.body: the 4 color ramp + shader swap is such a good call, thats basically how old games did palette swaps too. curious if the horn overlays ever fight the head outline when the goat flips direction? thats where mine usually broke

replies.author: Joe_Finback
replies.body:
Thanks! Yeah, same idea as the old palette swaps, just done in a shader.

The flip never fought me, because nothing flips on its own. The horn and bell are children of the goat node, placed in the right-facing space, and turning around just sets the whole node's scale.x to -1. The pivot sits on a pixel edge (x 16 on a 32 px canvas), so the mirror lands on whole pixels and the horn goes wherever the head goes.

The outline part was solved in the horn sprites themselves. Each one carries a 1 px ink margin, and its bottom ink row sits right on the skull's own outline row. Only the pixels under the horn's base get inked, so it never paints over the ear.

For me the fiddly part is squash and stretch, not the flip. The head anchor gets scaled and rounded to whole pixels separately from the body, so that's where a 1 px gap could show up. A frame-by-frame check of every horn through the full jump is still on my list.

Do you have sprites in all directions? did you try a 3d model underlying them?

replies.author: stolenyourgf
replies.body: nah no 3d under mine, its all hand drawn. i do 4 dirs and mirror for the rest, front first then back/side traced off it at low opacity. the 3/4 views are where it drifts most for me, head ends up a px wider lol
